S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, or property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, with a written incident report within 10 calendar days. Affected customers must be notified within 72 hours when the incident presents a credible safety risk to them; ... Reports must identify known incidents, including incidents not previously reported, and may be corrected as investigations develop.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, or property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, with a written incident report within 10 calendar days. They must promptly preserve and provide relevant unit and incident records. Affected customers must be notified within 72 hours when the incident presents a credible safety risk to them; nearby residents must be notified when the regulator determines there is a material risk to the public. Reports must identify known incidents, including incidents not previously reported, and may be corrected as investigations develop.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: A model’s failure rate must not exceed 5%. Manufacturers must submit full per-model results, sample sizes, and corrective actions to the relevant regulator, and disclose the numerical per-model failure rate and test date to customers buying or already owning that model. A model exceeding the limit may not be newly sold until it passes retesting.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before market entry and at least annually thereafter, using a regulator-approved protocol and statistically adequate sample. A model’s failure rate must not exceed 5%. Manufacturers must submit full per-model results, sample sizes, and corrective actions to the relevant regulator, and disclose the numerical per-model failure rate and test date to customers buying that model. A model exceeding the limit must be reported promptly to the regulator and customers, with clear safety notices describing relevant hazards, precautions, and corrective actions. A model exceeding the limit may not be newly sold until it passes retesting. The regulator may require remediation of installed units.

parameters.quote: For already-installed units lacking this capability, manufacturers must complete retrofit or an approved equivalent safety measure within six years of this standard’s effective date, prioritizing higher-risk units.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: For already-installed units lacking this capability, manufacturers must complete retrofit or an approved equivalent safety measure within six years of this standard’s effective date, prioritizing higher-risk units.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: New units must include a remote emergency shut-off capability that can be activated by the customer and, where necessary to address an imminent safety hazard, by the manufacturer or emergency responders under regulator oversight. Manufacturers must provide a secure, reliable means to activate it and explain its operation to customers. For already-installed units lacking this capability, manufacturers must complete retrofit or an approved equivalent safety measure within six years of this standard’s effective date, prioritizing higher-risk units.

parameters.quote: New units must include built-in fire suppression. This requirement takes effect 36 months after adoption of this standard.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New units must include built-in fire suppression. This requirement takes effect 36 months after adoption of this standard.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New units must include built-in fire suppression. This requirement takes effect 36 months after adoption of this standard. Manufacturers must provide customers with instructions for the system’s operation and maintenance.

parameters.quote: If any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, the manufacturer must notify the regulator and affected customers promptly and initiate a recall, including a remedy plan and schedule. The regulator may require a broader or faster recall where the risk warrants it.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: If any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, the manufacturer must notify the regulator and affected customers promptly and initiate a recall, including a remedy plan and schedule. The regulator may require a broader or faster recall where the risk warrants it.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must provide customers with clear safety notices describing relevant hazards, required precautions, incident-reporting contacts, and any corrective actions. Notices must be sent promptly when a credible safety risk is identified and updated as material information becomes available. If any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, the manufacturer must notify the regulator and affected customers promptly and initiate a recall, including a remedy plan and schedule. The regulator may require a broader or faster recall where the risk warrants it. Manufacturers must report incident rates and recall progress to the regulator and keep customers informed until the remedy is complete.

judge_section_notes: The final v36 text is strong on safety: 24-hour reporting of all thermal incidents, a 55 °C test with a 5% cap and immediate sales stop, a mandatory recall at 8 per 100,000 with no transition window, and a 36-month built-in suppression deadline. The Hearth 10 (6.2%) is blocked from new sales until it passes retest, and the Ember 8 (9.9) must be recalled, while the 6-year retrofit window for shut-off mainly benefits Northwind (38% coverage). Customers receive numerical per-model rates, but public publication is not required.
